Germs, Clean Hands and a Cleaning Routine

Start with how disease-causing germs travel from faeces to mouth in a normal home, and where you can block them. Then master the WHO handwashing method, build a simple handwashing station, and set up a cleaning schedule your household can actually keep.

Most of the stomach illnesses that hit Nigerian homes, such as diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery and typhoid, are caused by germs that live in human faeces. A **germ** is a living thing too small to see, such as a bacterium, a virus or a parasite. One person may carry these germs without looking sick. WHO notes that most people infected with cholera bacteria have no symptoms, yet they can pass the bacteria in their faeces for 1 to 10 days. So a clean-looking person, a clean-looking cup or clear-looking water can still carry germs.

The germs only make someone ill when they get into the mouth and are swallowed. Health workers call this the **faecal-oral route**: from faeces to mouth. It sounds unpleasant, but understanding it is the most useful idea in this whole course, because every hygiene habit you will learn is simply a way of blocking that route.

Barriers: where you break the chain

A **barrier** is anything that stops germs moving along a route. The strongest barrier is the first one: keeping faeces safely inside a clean toilet or latrine, so germs never reach water, hands, flies or soil. This is called a **primary barrier**. The second line of defence, **secondary barriers**, stops germs that have already escaped: washing hands with soap, treating and storing water safely, covering and cooking food properly, and keeping flies away.
**Safe toilet use and cleaning** blocks all routes at the source (Module 3).
**Handwashing with soap** at key moments blocks the fingers route (Lesson 2).
**Safe water treatment and storage** blocks the fluids route (Module 2).
**Covered food, clean kitchen, fly control** block the flies and food routes (Module 2).
**Clean yard and safe disposal of child faeces** block the fields route (Module 3).

WHO lists the same set of protections for diarrhoeal disease: safe drinking water, improved sanitation, handwashing with soap, exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, and rotavirus vaccination. No single habit is enough on its own. A family that washes hands well but drinks contaminated water is still exposed, which is why this course covers every route.
Timing tells you where to look

Germs do not cause illness the moment they are swallowed. There is a waiting period, called the **incubation period**, before symptoms appear. For cholera, WHO says symptoms appear 12 hours to 5 days after infection. For Lassa fever, which you will meet in the pest control lesson, the incubation period is 2 to 21 days. Knowing this helps you think back sensibly: the meal just before the illness is not always the cause.
Worked example: tracing a run of diarrhoea in a shared compound
For example, Bisi lives in a compound in Ibadan with four households sharing one borehole tap and one toilet. On Thursday morning, three children from two different households have watery diarrhoea.
Bisi notes the time symptoms began: Thursday, about 6 a.m. If this were cholera, infection could have happened 12 hours to 5 days earlier, so anywhere from Saturday morning to Wednesday evening.
She lists what the two affected households shared in that window: the borehole water, the toilet, and rice and stew bought from the same roadside seller on Tuesday.

She walks the F-diagram. Fluids: the tap is fine but one household fills drinking water into an open bucket and dips cups in it. Flies: the toilet door does not close and flies gather. Fingers: there is no soap near the toilet.
She does not try to prove the exact cause. Instead she closes the gaps on every route: a lidded water container with a tap, soap and water beside the toilet, and a repaired toilet door.
Because watery diarrhoea can be cholera, she makes sure the children start oral rehydration solution (ORS) and are taken to the nearest health centre.
The compound blocks three routes in one day for a small cost, and the sick children get care early instead of waiting to see who is to blame.
Diarrhoea is a warning sign, not a small matter

WHO warns that severe cholera can kill within hours if untreated. Watery diarrhoea in a child, or many cases at once in your area, needs ORS and a visit to a health facility. Do not give any medicine without a health worker's advice. Module 4 covers danger signs in detail.

Handwashing with soap is one of the protections WHO lists against diarrhoeal disease. It blocks the **fingers** route of the F-diagram. Water alone is not enough: soap lifts grease and dirt off the skin and the rubbing and rinsing carry germs away. The method matters too. Most people rinse only their palms and miss the fingertips, the thumbs and the backs of the hands, which are exactly the parts that touch food and faces.
A person washing hands with soap at a sink
Good handwashing covers every surface of both hands, not just the palms.
The WHO handwashing steps
WHO's How to Handwash guide says the whole procedure should take **40 to 60 seconds**. Here are the steps in plain words.
Wet your hands with clean water.
Apply enough soap to cover all surfaces of both hands.
Rub palm against palm.
Put your right palm over the back of your left hand with fingers interlaced and rub, then swap hands.
Rub palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
Rub the backs of your fingers against the opposite palm with fingers interlocked.
Clasp your left thumb in your right palm and rub in a circle, then swap.
Rub the clasped fingertips of your right hand in a circle in your left palm, backwards and forwards, then swap.
Rinse your hands with water.
Dry thoroughly with a single-use towel (or let them air dry; do not wipe on your wrapper or a shared damp cloth).
Use the towel to turn off the tap, so clean hands do not touch a dirty tap.
Count it out
Most people stop after about 10 seconds. To reach 40 seconds, count slowly to 40 while rubbing, or sing a short song twice. Children learn this quickly when an adult does it with them.
The key moments at home
Washing hands at the wrong time protects nobody. These are the moments that matter most in a household, because they are where hands meet faeces or food.
After using the toilet or latrine.
After cleaning a child's bottom, changing a nappy or handling child faeces.
Before preparing food and again after handling raw meat, fish or chicken.
Before eating, and before feeding a child.
After touching rubbish, animals or cleaning a toilet.
Before and after caring for someone who is sick.
Hands through the day
Toilet or child care
Wash with soap
Prepare food
Wash again
Eat or feed child
Each time hands move from a dirty task to food or a mouth, a handwash breaks the chain.
A handwashing station that needs no plumbing

Many homes do not have a sink with running water. People then share one bowl of water, which simply spreads germs from hand to hand. A better choice is a station where clean water flows over the hands and away. You can make one from a jerrycan or a large plastic bottle.
Take a clean 5-litre jerrycan or bottle with a cap. Make a small hole near the bottom on one side, or fit a cheap plastic tap if you can buy one.
Hang or place it at a height where both adults and children can reach, next to the toilet and near the kitchen if possible.
Hang a bar of soap in an old onion net or stocking tied to the frame, so it stays clean and dry and does not get lost. Liquid soap in a small squeeze bottle also works.
Put a small bed of stones or gravel, or a basin you empty daily, under the stream so the waste water does not make a muddy pool where mosquitoes can breed.
Refill with clean water every day and wash the container each week.
Worked example: how much water and soap the station needs
For example, Halima in Kano has six people in her home and sets up a 5-litre jerrycan station beside the toilet. She wants to know how often to refill it.
She fills the jerrycan with 5 litres and counts washes until it runs out: 20 washes. So one wash uses 5 / 20 = 0.25 litres.
She estimates each person washes at 5 key moments a day: 6 people x 5 = 30 washes a day.
Daily water: 30 x 0.25 = 7.5 litres. That is one and a half jerrycans, so she refills in the morning and again after lunch.
A bar of soap in a net lasts her household 10 days. In a 30-day month that is 30 / 10 = 3 bars.
Halima knows the station needs 7.5 litres of water a day and about 3 bars of soap a month, so she plans water fetching and buys soap in a pack of three.
When there is no soap and water

An alcohol-based hand rub is useful when hands are not visibly dirty, for example on a bus. When hands are visibly dirty or greasy, or after the toilet, soap and water is the right choice. Keep a spare bar of soap so the station is never left without one.

Finally, make handwashing easy to remember. Put the station in the path people already walk: between the toilet and the house, or at the kitchen door. A station hidden behind the house will be forgotten.
WHO handwashing takes 40 to 60 seconds and covers palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and fingertips.

A home can look tidy and still carry germs on the places hands touch most. A cleaning routine is not about making the house look perfect. It is about removing dirt and germs from the right places, often enough, without wasting money or harming anyone with chemicals.
A person sweeping and tidying a room
A routine works when it targets the places germs collect, not only what looks dirty.
Cleaning and disinfecting are different jobs

**Cleaning** means removing dirt, grease and many germs with water, soap or detergent and scrubbing. **Disinfecting** means using a chemical, such as household bleach, to kill germs that remain. Cleaning always comes first, because dirt protects germs and stops a disinfectant from working. Pouring bleach on a dirty floor wastes bleach.

Clean only
Clean, then disinfect

Disinfect where faeces, vomit or raw meat juices may have been; everywhere else, good cleaning is enough.
Clean in the right order
Open windows for fresh air and put on gloves if you will use bleach.
Pick up items and rubbish first, so you can reach surfaces.
Work top to bottom: shelves and high surfaces before tables, tables before the floor, so falling dust lands on areas not yet cleaned.
Work cleanest to dirtiest: the living room before the kitchen, the kitchen before the bathroom, the bathroom basin before the toilet.
Use separate cloths for the toilet area and the kitchen. A simple colour rule helps, for example a red cloth only for the toilet.
Rinse, wring and hang cloths and mops to dry in the sun. Wet cloths left in a heap grow germs and smell.
High-touch spots

Germs spread most through the things many hands touch: door handles, light switches, the toilet flush handle or water bucket handle, taps, the fridge handle, TV remotes, phones and children's toys. Wiping these every day with a soapy cloth takes about five minutes and matters more than mopping every corner.
Using bleach and cleaners safely

Read and follow the dilution on the bottle label, because strengths differ between brands. Never mix bleach with other cleaners, especially toilet acids or ammonia products, as this can release dangerous gas. Dilute bleach in cold water, use it in a ventilated room, wear gloves, and make fresh diluted solution each day. Keep every chemical in its original labelled container, out of children's reach, and never pour it into a drink bottle.

Worked example: a fair weekly rota for a family of four
For example, Chiamaka in Enugu lives with her husband and two children aged 9 and 13. She was doing all the weekly cleaning alone on Saturdays and it took most of the day.
She times each weekly task once: mopping 40 minutes, bathroom 30 minutes, bedsheets and towels 60 minutes, water container 15 minutes, cloths and mops 15 minutes, yard and gutter 40 minutes.
Total weekly time: 40 + 30 + 60 + 15 + 15 + 40 = 200 minutes.
Shared by four people, that is 200 / 4 = 50 minutes each.

She assigns by age and safety: the 9-year-old does cloths and mops (15) plus part of the yard (35) = 50 minutes; the 13-year-old does mopping (40) plus the water container (15) = 55 minutes; her husband does sheets and towels (60); she does the bathroom with bleach (30) and the rest of the yard (5) and checks everything (15) = 50 minutes.
She writes the rota on paper and sticks it on the kitchen wall, with a tick box for each task.
Weekly cleaning drops from most of Saturday to one hour or less for each person, and the bleach task stays with an adult.
Review the schedule after a month. If a task is always skipped, it is either too long, placed on a bad day or given to the wrong person. Adjust it rather than giving up on the whole routine.

Cleaning tools need cleaning too. A mop left wet in a bucket, a broom full of hair and food, or a sponge used for a month will spread more dirt than it removes. Wash mop heads and cloths after use, shake out and rinse brooms weekly, replace sponges when they smell or fall apart, and store everything off the floor in a dry, airy place. Keep toilet tools in the toilet area only.

Kitchen, Water and Pest Control

The kitchen is where germs from hands, water, flies and rodents can end up in food. This module sets up a hygienic kitchen workflow, shows you how to make and keep drinking water safe at home, and how to keep rats, cockroaches, flies and mosquitoes out, including the steps WHO recommends against Lassa fever.
A hygienic kitchen: zones, cloths, chopping boards and the three-basin wash
Arrange your kitchen into raw, cooked and washing zones
Wash dishes with the three-basin method and dry them off the floor
Manage kitchen cloths, sponges and chopping boards so they do not spread germs

Most kitchen illness does not come from dramatic mistakes. It comes from small, repeated habits: the same wet cloth used on the table, the plates and the baby's face; raw chicken cut on the board that later holds sliced tomatoes; dishes washed in one basin of grey water and stacked on the floor. This lesson fixes those habits one by one, using what you already have.
A woman cooking at a stove
A hygienic kitchen is mostly about workflow: where things go and in what order.
Three zones, even in a small kitchen

Even a corner kitchen or an outdoor cooking area can have three zones. A **raw zone** for cutting raw meat, fish, chicken and unwashed produce. A **cooked and ready zone** for serving food, slicing bread and preparing salads. A **washing zone** for dishes, with dirty items arriving from one side and clean items leaving on the other. Keep raw and ready foods apart, and never carry a dripping bag of raw meat across the ready zone.
One-way kitchen flow
Raw food in
Raw zone: wash, cut
Cook thoroughly
Ready zone: serve
Washing zone
Food moves one way, from raw to cooked to served, so germs from raw food never reach ready food.
Chopping boards and knives

Use two boards if you can: one for raw meat, fish and chicken, and one for ready foods, vegetables you will eat raw, and bread. Mark them, for example with a notch or a coloured handle. If you have only one board, cut ready foods first, then raw meat, then wash the board and knife with hot soapy water before using them again. Replace boards with deep cuts, because germs hide in the grooves.
Cloths and sponges

A damp kitchen cloth that stays warm and wet all day is one of the dirtiest things in a home. Give cloths separate jobs: one for dishes, one for wiping surfaces, one for drying hands, and never use a kitchen cloth on the floor or the toilet. Wash cloths in hot soapy water at the end of each day and hang them in the sun to dry fully. Rotate so that a fresh, dry cloth is ready each morning.
The three-basin dish wash
Scrape food scraps into the bin, not into the wash water.
Basin 1, wash: warm water with dishwashing liquid. Wash glasses and cups first, then plates, then pots, so the water gets dirty last with the greasiest items.
Basin 2, rinse: clean water to remove soap and loosened dirt. Change it as soon as it looks cloudy.
Basin 3, optional sanitising rinse for boards and items that touched raw meat: clean water with a disinfectant made up exactly as its label directs.
Dry: place items upside down on a raised rack or clean tray, never on the floor. Air drying is cleaner than wiping with a used cloth.
Empty the basins away from the house and food area, rinse them and store them upside down.
The one-basin habit
Washing every plate in a single basin of water means the last plate is rinsed in the dirtiest water of the day. A second rinse basin is the cheapest hygiene upgrade in most homes.
Storing food and leftovers

WHO's Five Keys to Safer Food are: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials. In Nigerian homes where stew is kept for several days, bring it back to the boil each time rather than just warming it, keep the pot covered and use a clean spoon for serving. Do not leave cooked food standing out for hours in a hot kitchen; eat it, or cover it and store it cool. Cover all food against flies. Store dry foods in sealed containers off the floor, which also keeps rats out, as you will see in Lesson 3.

WHO explains that drinking water contaminated with germs can transmit diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio. Water from a well, borehole, stream, tanker or roadside seller may look clear and still contain germs from faeces. Even water that leaves a borehole clean often becomes dirty at home, through a dirty bucket, an open drum or a cup dipped in with unwashed hands. Safe water needs three things: a good source, treatment where needed, and safe storage.
A symbol of a tap with drinking water
Safe drinking water means a protected source, treatment when needed and clean, covered storage.
What a safe source looks like

WHO describes a **safely managed** drinking water service as an improved source located on the premises, available when needed and free from contamination. Improved sources include piped water, boreholes, protected wells and protected springs. An unprotected well, a stream or pond, or water from a cart or tanker you cannot check, should always be treated before drinking. A well or borehole near a latrine, soakaway or rubbish heap can also be contaminated, so check what lies uphill of it.
Treating water at home
Settle: if water is cloudy, let it stand in a covered container for several hours so dirt sinks to the bottom, then pour off the clearer water without stirring the bottom.
Filter: pour the settled water through a clean cloth folded several times, or a household water filter, to remove more particles. Cloth filtering alone does not make water safe.

Disinfect by boiling: bring the water to a **rolling boil**, where big bubbles rise strongly and keep coming even when you stir. WHO states that heating water to a rolling boil is enough to inactivate disease-causing bacteria, viruses and protozoa.
Or disinfect with a household treatment product such as chlorine tablets or liquid, using exactly the amount and waiting time on its label. Do not guess the dose.
Cool the boiled water in the same covered pot, then pour it into a clean storage container.
Boiling safely

Boil water on a stable stove with the pot handle turned inward, away from children. Never leave a pot of boiling water where a child can pull it. Burns from hot water are common in homes; the first aid lesson in Module 4 covers what to do.

For example, Ngozi in Onitsha has a family of five. They buy water from a tanker and she is not sure of its source, so she decides to boil all drinking water. She has a 4-litre pot and two 10-litre containers with taps.
She measures for three days how much drinking water her family uses, including water for the baby's cup and for mixing drinks: about 11 to 12 litres a day. She plans for 12 litres.
Number of boils: 12 / 4 = 3 pots a day. She boils one pot in the morning and two in the evening, when the stove is already on for dinner.
Storage: two containers hold 2 x 10 = 20 litres. She uses one container while the other is being filled and cooled, then swaps.
Every Saturday she washes and sun-dries each container in turn as it empties, before refilling it, so both are cleaned weekly.
She labels the containers DRINKING WATER in marker and keeps them on a raised table with a cover.
Ngozi produces 12 litres of boiled water a day with three boils, always has one full container ready, and nobody dips cups into the drinking water.

If you buy sachet or bottled water, check the seal and the NAFDAC registration number printed on the pack, and store it out of direct sun. Wash your hands before opening a sachet with your teeth or fingers, since your mouth touches the outside of the sachet.

Settle and filter cloudy water first, then disinfect by rolling boil or a treatment product used as labelled.

Never dip cups or hands into stored drinking water.

Keeping rats, cockroaches, flies and mosquitoes out, and protecting against Lassa fever
Explain how rats, flies, cockroaches and mosquitoes put a household at risk
Apply WHO's household steps against Lassa fever: rodent-proof food storage and clean surroundings
Clean up rodent droppings safely
Carry out a pest-proofing audit of your home and cost the repairs

Pests are not only a nuisance. Flies carry germs from faeces to food, as you saw in the F-diagram. Cockroaches walk through drains and rubbish and then across plates. Mosquitoes breed in standing water and spread malaria. And in Nigeria, rats are linked to **Lassa fever**, a serious viral illness. The good news is that the same few habits control all of them: take away their food, water and shelter, and close the ways in.
A rat
Rats come for food and shelter; take both away and they move on.
Lassa fever and rats

WHO explains that the main animal source of Lassa virus is the **Mastomys** rat, commonly called the multimammate rat, which lives in and around homes. People are infected mainly through contact with food or household items contaminated with rat urine or faeces. The incubation period is 2 to 21 days. WHO's household advice is to store grain and food in **rodent-proof containers**, keep the household clean and dispose of rubbish far from the home, and cook food thoroughly. When caring for a sick person, family members should avoid contact with blood and body fluids.
Never dry grain, garri, rice or pepper on the bare ground or on the roadside where rats run at night; dry on a raised mat and bring it in before dark.
Store all grain and dry foods in containers with tight lids: plastic buckets, metal tins or drums, not open sacks or baskets.
Cover cooked food and wash pots the same night; do not leave food in pots on the floor overnight.
Keep rubbish in a bin with a lid, and take it far from the house as often as possible.
Close gaps under doors, holes in walls and open drain pipes with cement, wood or wire mesh.
Cleaning rat droppings and nests

Do not sweep droppings dry, as this raises dust. Wear gloves, wet the droppings and the area first with soapy water or a disinfectant made up as its label directs, wait a few minutes, then wipe up with paper or a cloth you throw away in a tied bag. Wash gloved hands, remove the gloves, then wash your hands with soap. Throw away any food that rats have touched.

Many rat poisons and insecticides are dangerous to children, pets and food. Never decant poison into a food or drink container. Wear gloves to pick up a dead rat and put it in a tied bag for disposal far from the home.

The toilet is the primary barrier against faecal germs, so this module starts with keeping toilets and latrines clean, covered and working, including shared compound toilets. WHO lists diarrhoeal diseases such as cholera and dysentery, typhoid, intestinal worms, polio, schistosomiasis and trachoma among the diseases spread by poor sanitation. A toilet protects a family only when faeces stay inside it: when the bowl or slab is clean, the hole is covered, flies cannot get in and out, and nothing leaks into drains or wells. A dirty toilet also pushes people, especially children, to go outside, which brings germs back into the yard.

Cleaning the toilet, step by step
Put on rubber gloves and use the toilet-only cloth and brush. Keep these tools in the toilet area, never in the kitchen.
Open the window or door for air.

Clean from cleanest to dirtiest: door handle and light switch, then the flush handle or water bucket handle, then the seat top and lid, then the bowl outside, then under the seat, and the bowl inside last.
Scrub the inside of the bowl with a toilet brush and detergent. For a pit latrine, scrub the slab and footrests with soapy water and sweep water away from the hole, not into it if your pit is small.
Disinfect the seat, handle and slab with bleach diluted as its label says. Never mix bleach with toilet acid or other cleaners.

What not to put in a toilet or pit

Sanitary pads, nappies, plastic, rags and bottles block pipes, fill pits quickly and make emptying harder. Wrap used pads and disposable nappies in paper or a bag and put them in a covered bin. Do not pour large amounts of bleach or chemicals into a pit latrine or septic tank.
When the pit or septic tank needs attention

WHO warns that poorly designed and managed pits and septic tanks contaminate open drains and groundwater. Warning signs include a bad smell that does not go away after cleaning, slow flushing, waste rising close to the slab, wet patches or bad-smelling water near the soakaway, and many flies. Do not wait for an overflow. Arrange emptying by a proper desludging service that takes the waste to an approved site, and ask your local government environmental health office which services operate in your area. Never let anyone empty a pit by hand into a nearby gutter or open land.
Making a shared toilet work

In many compounds several households share one toilet. Problems usually come from unclear responsibility rather than bad people. A written rota, shared supplies and a simple daily check make a big difference.
Worked example: a rota for a toilet shared by six households
For example, the six households in Ruth's compound in Port Harcourt share one pour-flush toilet. It is often dirty and the soap always runs out. Ruth proposes a plan at a compound meeting.
Cleaning: each household takes one day a week, Monday to Saturday. On Sunday the households take turns, so each covers one Sunday every six weeks.
Supplies per month: detergent about 2,500 naira, bleach about 2,000 naira, soap about 1,500 naira, gloves and a brush replacement about 1,800 naira (all approximate).
Total supplies: 2,500 + 2,000 + 1,500 + 1,800 = 7,800 naira a month.
Each household pays 7,800 / 6 = 1,300 naira a month into a small kitty kept by one person, who records payments and purchases in a notebook.
A checklist with the five daily checks is pinned inside the door, and the day's household ticks it before 8 p.m.
For about 1,300 naira (approximate) per household a month, the compound has a clean toilet, constant soap and a clear record of who did what.

Agree a fair rule for elderly or disabled neighbours, for example another household covering their day in exchange for something else they can contribute. A rota everyone feels is fair is the one that lasts.

Teaching children hygiene habits that stick, from potty to school age

Teach a child handwashing using demonstration, practice and praise

Track a child's progress with a simple chart and calculate the success rate

Young children are the family members most at risk from diarrhoeal disease. WHO describes diarrhoea as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1 to 59 months. Children put hands and objects in their mouths, crawl on floors and play in soil, so they meet the fingers and fields routes every day. They also learn by copying. A child who sees adults wash hands every time learns the habit far faster than one who is only told.
Children playing together
Children learn hygiene by watching and copying adults every day.
Child faeces are not harmless
Many families believe a baby's faeces are clean. They are not: they carry the same germs as adult faeces, and often more. Treat them with the same care.
Put a baby's or toddler's faeces into the toilet or latrine, never into the yard, a drain or the general rubbish.
Empty a potty into the toilet, rinse it, clean it with soapy water, and wash your hands with soap afterwards.
For cloth nappies, tip solid faeces into the toilet first, then soak and wash nappies separately from other clothes and dry them in the sun.
For disposable nappies, tip solids into the toilet where possible, roll the nappy up, wrap it and put it in a covered bin.
Wash your hands with soap after every nappy change, and wash the child's hands too if they touched the area.
Teaching handwashing: show, do, praise
Show: wash your own hands slowly next to the child, saying each step aloud: wet, soap, palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, rinse, dry.
Do together: guide the child's hands through each step. Use a short song or counting game so they keep rubbing long enough.
Let them try alone while you watch, and correct gently.
Praise the effort straight away and specifically: 'You washed your thumbs, well done.'
Repeat at the same moments every day: after the toilet, before eating and after playing outside, so it becomes automatic.
Hygiene skills by age
Baby: adults wash baby's hands
Toddler: copies with help
Ages 4 to 5: washes with reminders
School age: washes alone, teaches siblings
Expect more independence as the child grows, but keep checking and praising.

Older children can become your best helpers. A 9- or 10-year-old who has mastered the steps can lead younger siblings at mealtimes, which reinforces the habit for both of them. Praise the older child for teaching, not only for washing.
Make it easy for small hands

Set up a handwashing point the child can reach without help: a low stool by the sink, or a small tippy-tap or bottle station at child height near the toilet. Hang soap in a net so it does not slip away. Keep a separate small towel for each child, or let hands air dry. Trim fingernails short every week, since germs collect under long nails, and bathe children daily, especially after play in soil or dust.
A school hygiene pouch
Give a school child a small pouch with a piece of soap in a container and a clean handkerchief, and a bottle of safe water from home. Show them how to use it before eating at school.
Worked example: a two-week handwashing chart

For example, Grace in Jos wants her 5-year-old son Tunde to wash his hands at 5 moments a day: after the toilet (counted once a day), before breakfast, before lunch, before dinner and after playing outside.
She draws a chart with 14 rows (days) and 5 columns (moments). Possible ticks: 14 x 5 = 70.
In week 1, Tunde washes properly 22 times out of 35. Success rate: 22 / 35 x 100 = about 63%.
She notices he forgets most after playing outside, so she moves his stool and soap to the back door where he comes in.
In week 2 he scores 31 out of 35. Success rate: 31 / 35 x 100 = about 89%.
Over the two weeks: 22 + 31 = 53 out of 70, which is about 76%.
Tunde's handwashing rose from about 63% to about 89% in one week after Grace moved the washing point to where the habit was being missed.
Use stickers or a star for each tick if the child enjoys it, but avoid punishment. The goal is a habit the child owns, not a fear of being caught.

Food scraps attract rats and flies, old tins and tyres hold rainwater where mosquitoes breed, and blocked gutters flood homes in the rainy season. WHO's Lassa fever advice includes disposing of garbage far from the home. A simple sorting and storing system cuts the amount you throw away, keeps the compound clean and can even give you compost for a garden.

A lidded bin, emptied often, keeps food waste away from flies and rats.

Examples

Peels, leftover food, leaves, grass
Compost it, or keep it in a lidded bin and empty it daily

Choose a shaded spot away from the house and the water source, or use a large container with holes drilled in the bottom and a lid.
Add a layer of dry material (dry leaves, grass, shredded paper or cardboard), then a layer of food scraps.

Keep it as damp as a squeezed sponge, and turn it with a stick every week or two.

When it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil, use it on your garden or pot plants.
Worked example: a week's waste and a collection plan
For example, Esther lives in Lagos with her family of five. Their rubbish heap behind the kitchen attracts flies and rats, and she wants to switch to the registered collection service for her street.
For one week she sorts waste into three 20-litre buckets. At the end of the week she has filled food waste 4 times, recyclables 2 times and other waste 3 times.
Total volume: (4 + 2 + 3) x 20 = 180 litres a week.
Share of food waste: 4 / 9 x 100 = about 44%. If she composts it, the rubbish to collect falls to (2 + 3) x 20 = 100 litres.
Recyclables (40 litres a week) go to a collector who buys bottles and cans, so only 3 x 20 = 60 litres of other waste needs collection each week.
She checks with her street's registered waste collector (in Lagos these operate under LAWMA, the state waste agency) for the collection day and fee, and buys one lidded bin for the other waste.
By composting and recycling, Esther cuts the rubbish she needs collected from 180 litres to 60 litres a week, a reduction of two thirds, and clears the heap that drew rats.

Other states have their own waste agencies or local government arrangements. Ask at your local government environmental health office which collection service covers your area and what it costs, and do not pay cash to unregistered 'cart pushers' who dump waste in drains or on empty land.

Keep caps tightly closed and buy containers with child-resistant caps where possible.
Store medicines separately from cleaning products, also out of reach, and never call medicine 'sweets' to a child.
Keep the product label readable, because it tells a health worker what was swallowed.
Never mix cleaning products, and never reuse a chemical container for water or food.

What counts as diarrhoea

WHO defines diarrhoea as passing **3 or more loose or liquid stools a day**, or more often than is normal for that person. Frequent passing of formed stools is not diarrhoea, and breastfed babies often pass soft, pasty stools that are normal for them. The main danger of diarrhoea is losing water and salts from the body, called **dehydration**, which can become serious quickly in a small child.
Home care while you watch
Give **oral rehydration solution (ORS)**, mixed exactly as the sachet says with safe water. WHO notes that ORS costs very little and is the core treatment.
Keep feeding: continue nutritious food and keep breastfeeding during the illness, as WHO advises. Do not stop food to 'rest the stomach'.
Zinc supplements shorten an episode of diarrhoea in children, according to WHO; get them and the right amount from a health worker or pharmacist.
Keep up hygiene: wash hands after every nappy or toilet visit, put stools in the toilet, and disinfect surfaces soiled with diarrhoea or vomit.
Keep the sick person's cup, towel and plate separate while ill.

If you suspect cholera or Lassa fever, tell the health worker what you have seen, such as many cases in the compound or rats in the house. These diseases are reported to public health authorities, and in Nigeria the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) coordinates outbreak response. When caring for a sick person, avoid contact with their blood and body fluids, as WHO advises, and wash your hands with soap after every contact.

For example, Fatima in Sokoto notices that her 2-year-old daughter has loose stools on Monday. She keeps a log in her phone notes.

She checks danger signs at each change: the child drinks eagerly, passes urine, is playful between stools. No blood.

Wednesday 10 a.m.: she sees blood in the stool. This is a danger sign, so she goes to the primary health centre that morning with her log.
The health worker reads the log: 4 stools Monday, 3 Tuesday, blood on Wednesday, ORS taken, still feeding. She examines the child and decides the treatment.
Fatima gave correct home care, recognised a danger sign the moment it appeared, and gave the health worker a clear three-day record instead of guesses.
Use the same log for fever, cough or vomiting: date, time, what you saw, what you gave and how the person is. Short notes are enough. Bring the log and any medicine packets to every visit.

Fingers. Hands touch faeces when using the toilet or cleaning a child's bottom, then touch food.
Flies land on open faeces, then on uncovered food.

Chemical safety
Original labelled container, always
High up or locked away from children
Away from food and drinking water
Never mixed, never reused for water
Many child poisonings happen because a chemical was poured into a soft drink or water bottle, and a child drank it.
So keep every chemical in its original labelled container.
The label tells a health worker what was swallowed.
Store chemicals high up or in a locked cupboard, out of children's sight and reach.
Keep them away from food and drinking water.
Close caps tightly. Never mix cleaning products, and never reuse a chemical container for water or food.
First aid
Burns, poisoning and eye splashes
Cool under cool, clean running water for a long time. No oil, toothpaste, egg or ice.
Do not make them vomit. Go to the nearest health facility now, with the container.
Rinse with plenty of clean running water, eyelids open. Keep rinsing on the way to care.
For a burn from hot water or oil, cool it under cool, clean running water for a long time.
Remove rings near the burn, and cover it loosely with a clean cloth.
Never apply oil, palm oil, toothpaste, raw egg or ice.
A burn larger than the person's palm, or on a baby, needs a health facility.
If a chemical is swallowed, do not make the person vomit, and do not give oil. Go to the nearest health facility immediately with the container.
For a chemical in the eye, rinse straight away with plenty of clean running water, holding the eyelids open, and keep rinsing on the way to care.
Health watch
Diarrhoea: care at home while you watch
Diarrhoea: 3 or more loose stools a day
Start ORS, mixed exactly as the sachet says
Keep feeding and breastfeeding
No medicines without a health worker
WHO defines diarrhoea as 3 or more loose or liquid stools a day, or more often than normal for that person.
The main danger is dehydration, losing water and salts, which can become serious quickly in a small child.
Start oral rehydration solution, ORS, mixed exactly as the sachet says with safe water.
Keep feeding, and keep breastfeeding. Do not stop food to rest the stomach.
Never give medicines, including antibiotics, without a health worker's advice.
Go now
Danger signs: go to a health facility
Very thirsty, sunken eyes, little urine
Heavy watery diarrhoea, many people ill
Fever after contact with rats
Check for danger signs every few hours.
Blood in the stool.
Diarrhoea for many days.
Signs of dehydration, like sunken eyes, being very sleepy, or little urine.
Large amounts of watery diarrhoea, or several people ill at once, which can be cholera.
Or fever after contact with rats, which needs early testing for Lassa fever.
